normal.stem:
You have an Azure Machine Learning compute cluster that trains on data in an Azure Storage account.

Security forbids account keys and SAS tokens. You need the training jobs to read the data.

What should you do?
opts: Save the account key in the workspace Key Vault, and read it from the training script
Set the container's public access level to Blob, so the cluster can read it anonymously
Generate a SAS token that expires in one year, and register it in the datastore
Assign a managed identity to the cluster, and grant it Storage Blob Data Reader on the account
normal.rationale: A managed identity authenticates without a stored secret, and Storage Blob Data Reader gives the read access the jobs need. An account key and a SAS token are both secrets, even when kept in Key Vault or a datastore. A public container removes authentication altogether.
normal.hint: No secrets + Azure resource = managed identity + a data role.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Set up authentication between Azure Machine Learning and other services

normal.stem:
You register an Azure Machine Learning datastore for a blob container.

The security team requires that no secret is stored in the workspace for this datastore.

Which authentication method should you use?
opts: Service principal with a client secret, stored in the datastore definition
SAS token, stored in the datastore definition
Identity-based access, with no credential stored in the datastore
Account key, stored in the datastore definition
normal.rationale: Credential-less (identity-based) datastores rely on Microsoft Entra identities and Azure RBAC, so nothing secret is saved. Account keys, SAS tokens and service principal secrets are all stored credentials.
normal.hint: Credential-less datastore = identity-based access, no stored secret.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Set up authentication between Azure Machine Learning and other services

normal.stem:
A folder in Azure Data Lake Storage contains Parquet files. The training script must load them as a single pandas DataFrame that keeps only five columns.

You want consumers to use the data without writing any parsing code.

Which data asset should you create?
opts: A custom_model asset that stores the Parquet files with the model
An mltable asset that defines the Parquet source and a keep_columns step
A uri_folder asset that points to the folder, and each consumer parses the files
A uri_file asset that points to one Parquet file in the folder
normal.rationale: An mltable asset stores the loading logic (source files, column selection, other transformations) next to the data, so consumers call one load function and get a table. A uri_folder or uri_file only gives a path, and every consumer has to write the parsing code. A model asset is for models.
normal.hint: Table with schema and transformations = mltable. Just a path = uri_file or uri_folder.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
Training runs on different days produce different results, because the conda file for your Azure Machine Learning environment does not pin package versions.

You need runs to be reproducible.

What should you do?
opts: Install the latest packages with pip at the start of the training script on every run
Install the packages manually on the compute cluster nodes before each training run
Pin the package versions in the conda file, and reference the registered environment by version
Reference the environment without a version, so the newest environment build is always picked up
normal.rationale: Pinned package versions in a registered, versioned environment mean every job builds the same image. Installing at job start or by hand pulls whatever is newest at that moment, and referring to the newest environment version removes the control you wanted.
normal.hint: Reproducible = pinned packages + a registered environment version.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
Your team built a data preparation component in workspace A. Teams that use workspaces B and C in other regions must reuse the same versioned component.

What should you do?
opts: Give the other teams the Contributor role on workspace A, and have them run it there
Copy the component code into workspaces B and C, and rename it in each one
Email the component YAML file to the other teams, and let each team create it
Register the component in a registry, and reference it from workspaces B and C
normal.rationale: A registry is built to share assets such as components, environments and models across workspaces, and it keeps versions. Copies drift apart, and Contributor on workspace A gives far more access than reuse needs.
normal.hint: Share assets across workspaces = registry.

normal.stem:
You need to make an Azure Machine Learning workspace unreachable from the public internet.

Which TWO actions should you take?
opts: Assign a public IP address to the compute cluster
Create a private endpoint for the workspace in your virtual network
Add the corporate IP range to the workspace firewall allowlist
Set public network access on the workspace to Disabled
Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud on the subscription
normal.rationale: Disabling public network access closes the public endpoint, and a private endpoint gives users inside the virtual network a private path to the workspace. An IP allowlist keeps the public endpoint reachable. A public IP on compute and Defender for Cloud do not restrict workspace access.
normal.hint: No public access = disable public network access + private endpoint.

Your team deploys Azure Machine Learning infrastructure with a Bicep file. In each pull request, a check must list which resources would be created, changed or deleted, without changing anything in Azure.

Which command should the check run?
normal.rationale: what-if previews the changes a deployment would make and applies nothing. create deploys for real, and with Complete mode it can delete resources. bicep build only compiles to an ARM template. validate checks that the template can deploy, but it does not list the changes.
normal.hint: Preview changes without deploying = what-if.

opts: It creates a new storage account named by storageName, and then creates a role assignment
It references a storage account that already exists, and scopes a role assignment to it
It deletes and recreates the storage account named by storageName, and then creates a role assignment
It creates a role assignment at subscription scope, and ignores the storage account reference
normal.rationale: The existing keyword tells Bicep to look up a resource that is already deployed instead of creating it. The role assignment then uses that account as its scope, so the assignment applies to that account only.

normal.stem:
A faulty commit was pushed to the shared main branch of your ML repository, and teammates have already pulled it.

You need to undo its changes while keeping the existing history intact.

What should you do?
opts: Run git revert on the commit, and push the new revert commit
Run git commit --amend on the faulty commit, and force-push
Use an interactive rebase to drop the commit, and force-push
Run git reset --hard HEAD~1, and force-push
normal.rationale: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so shared history stays intact for everyone who pulled. reset, rebase and amend rewrite history, and force-pushing a rewritten main branch breaks teammates' copies.
normal.hint: Undo on a shared branch = revert. Rewriting history = reset, rebase, amend.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
Data scientists must be able to submit training jobs and register models in an Azure Machine Learning workspace.

They must not be able to create or delete compute resources or change workspace settings.

Which built-in role should you assign?
opts: Reader (read-only access to the workspace and its assets)
Owner (full access, including assigning roles to others)
AzureML Data Scientist (workspace actions, but no compute management)
Contributor (manage all resources, including compute and settings)
normal.rationale: AzureML Data Scientist allows nearly all workspace actions except creating or deleting compute and changing the workspace itself. Owner and Contributor allow those actions too, and Reader is read-only, so jobs could not be submitted.
normal.hint: Run jobs but not manage compute = AzureML Data Scientist.

A training script run on a laptop calls `mlflow.log_metric("auc", 0.91)`, but the metric never appears in the Azure Machine Learning workspace.

You need the metric to be logged to the workspace.

What should you do before logging?
opts: Call mlflow.autolog() to log automatically to the workspace
Register the metric as a model asset in the workspace
Replace log_metric with print statements, and parse the job logs
Call mlflow.set_tracking_uri with the workspace's tracking URI
normal.rationale: Outside Azure Machine Learning compute, MLflow does not know where the workspace is, so you point it at the workspace's tracking URI.

You use automated machine learning for a binary classification model that detects fraud. Only 0.5% of the training rows are fraud.

Which primary metric is the most appropriate?
normal.rationale: With a very small positive class, accuracy looks excellent even for a model that predicts no fraud at all. AUC_weighted still reflects how well the classes are separated. The other two are regression metrics.
normal.hint: Imbalanced classes: avoid accuracy, use AUC_weighted or similar.

normal.stem:
You define a sweep job. The search space samples learning_rate from a Normal distribution and batch_size from a Choice.

Which sampling algorithm can you use?
normal.rationale: Random sampling supports discrete and continuous search spaces. Grid supports only Choice, and Bayesian supports only Choice, Uniform and QUniform. Median stopping is an early termination policy, not a sampling algorithm.
normal.hint: Normal/LogUniform (continuous) = random. Grid = Choice only.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Hyperparameter tuning a model (v2)

normal.stem: Match each early termination policy to what it does.

slots.label: Cancels trials whose primary metric is not within a slack factor of the best trial
Cancels trials whose primary metric is worse than the median of the running averages of all trials
Cancels a fixed percentage of the lowest-performing trials at each evaluation interval

normal.rationale: Bandit compares each trial with the best one using slack_factor or slack_amount. Median stopping compares with the median of running averages. Truncation selection drops a percentage (truncation_percentage) of the worst trials at each interval. Sobol is a sampling option, not a policy.
normal.hint: Bandit = slack from best. Median = vs median. Truncation = bottom percent.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
A sweep job must run at most 20 trials, at most 4 at the same time, and the whole sweep must stop after one hour.

Which call meets the requirements?
normal.rationale: max_total_trials caps the number of trials, max_concurrent_trials caps how many run in parallel, and timeout is in seconds for the whole sweep, so one hour is 3600. The other calls swap the two limits, use 60 seconds, or let all 20 trials run at once.
normal.hint: total = how many, concurrent = at once, timeout = seconds for the whole sweep.

normal.stem:
You must run a PyTorch distributed training job on 2 nodes. Each node has 4 GPUs.

Which command job settings should you use?
opts: instance_count=2, with distribution type PyTorch and process_count_per_instance=4
instance_count=2, with distribution type PyTorch and process_count_per_instance=1
instance_count=1, with distribution type PyTorch and process_count_per_instance=8
instance_count=4, with distribution type PyTorch and process_count_per_instance=2
normal.rationale: instance_count sets the number of nodes (2), and process_count_per_instance sets how many processes run on each node, usually one per GPU (4). The other settings give the wrong number of nodes or leave GPUs unused.
normal.hint: Nodes = instance_count. Processes per node = process_count_per_instance (one per GPU).

normal.stem:
An Azure Machine Learning pipeline has a first step that downloads the latest records from an external API. When you rerun the pipeline with the same inputs, the step is skipped and the old data is used.

You need the step to run every time.

What should you do?
opts: Set is_deterministic to false on the component
Rename the pipeline job on every run
Convert the step into a sweep job
Increase the maximum number of nodes in the compute cluster
normal.rationale: Pipelines can reuse the output of a previous run when a deterministic component and its inputs are unchanged. A step that reads changing external data must declare is_deterministic false so it always runs.
normal.hint: Step reads changing external data = is_deterministic false.

normal.stem:
A model was trained and logged with MLflow. You must deploy it to a managed online endpoint with the least effort.

What should you do?
opts: Write a score.py file with init and run functions, and build a custom environment
Build a Docker image, and push it to Azure Container Registry
Convert the model to ONNX, and deploy it with a custom container
Register it as an MLflow model, and deploy it without a scoring script or a custom environment
normal.rationale: MLflow models support no-code deployment, so Azure Machine Learning generates the scoring logic and environment from the model metadata. The other choices add work that is not needed.
normal.hint: MLflow model = no-code deployment, no score.py.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

You need to retire version 3 of a registered model so teams stop selecting it, but you want to keep its lineage and artifacts.

What should you do?
opts: Register the same artifacts again under a new model name
Delete the model and its artifacts
Delete the storage container that holds the artifacts
normal.rationale: Archiving hides the version from the default listings while it remains in the workspace, so lineage is kept and the version can still be referenced. Deleting artifacts or their storage destroys what you wanted to keep.
normal.hint: Retire but keep lineage = archive.

You use the Responsible AI dashboard to evaluate a loan approval model. You must compare accuracy and selection rate across groups defined by a sensitive feature.

Which component should you use?

normal.rationale: The fairness assessment compares model performance and outcomes, such as accuracy and selection rate, across groups defined by sensitive features. Counterfactual what-if looks at how changing features affects predictions. The model overview shows overall performance unless a sensitive feature is defined.

normal.stem:
Your online endpoint has a blue deployment and a green deployment that receives 20% of live traffic. The error rate of green spikes.

You need the fastest rollback without redeploying anything.

What should you do?
opts: Scale green down to zero instances, and keep the 20% traffic split
Delete the endpoint and recreate it with only the blue deployment
Set the endpoint traffic to 100% for blue and 0% for green
Redeploy the blue model to a new deployment name, and switch clients
normal.rationale: The traffic split is a property of the endpoint, so setting blue to 100% immediately stops sending requests to green.
normal.hint: Rollback = move traffic back to the old deployment.

Every night, 40 million records must be scored. Nobody waits for the results, and the output is written to storage.

Which option is the most appropriate?
opts: An Azure Functions timer trigger that calls an online endpoint
A managed online endpoint with autoscale
normal.rationale: Batch endpoints are built for asynchronous scoring of large datasets with outputs written to storage. Online endpoints are for real-time, low-latency requests.
normal.hint: Big asynchronous scoring = batch endpoint. Per-request low latency = online endpoint.

normal.stem:
You created a model monitor for a model on a managed online endpoint, but the data drift signal shows no production data.

What is the most likely missing configuration?
opts: The data drift threshold is set too high for the monitored features
The reference data is the validation dataset instead of the training data
Feature attribution drift is not turned on in the monitor settings
Production inference data collection is not enabled on the deployment
normal.rationale: Model monitoring computes signals from production inference data, so the deployment must collect it.
normal.hint: No data in the monitor = turn on inference data collection.

sources.title: Azure Machine Learning model monitoring

normal.stem:
A training loop is shown below. The training loss becomes unstable and does not improve.

```
for epoch in range(10):
    for x, y in loader:
        loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
```

What is the problem?
opts: optimizer.zero_grad() is never called, so gradients accumulate across batches
loss.backward() must be wrapped in torch.no_grad() to avoid storing activations
The loop must call optimizer.step() before loss.backward() on every batch
The optimizer must be Adam instead of SGD, because SGD cannot train this model
normal.rationale: PyTorch adds new gradients to the old ones, so without zero_grad each update uses the sum of all earlier batches. In the training loop, optimizer.step() comes after loss.backward().
normal.hint: PyTorch loop order: zero_grad, forward, backward, step.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam. Docs don't confirm: the cited tutorial shows zero_grad() before backward() and step(), but does not state that gradients accumulate without it.

normal.stem:
An agent in a Foundry project must query an index in Azure AI Search without API keys.

What should you do?
opts: Give the managed identity the Search Service Contributor role, and enable role-based access control
Put the search query key in the agent's app settings, and rotate it every 90 days
Give the project's managed identity the Search Index Data Reader role, and enable role-based access control
Store the search admin key in Key Vault, and have the agent read it at runtime to query the index
normal.rationale: Search Index Data Reader lets an identity query indexes, which is all the agent needs, and the search service must accept role-based access. Search Service Contributor manages the service and its objects but does not allow querying an index. Keys, even in Key Vault, are secrets.
normal.hint: Keyless Search queries = managed identity + Search Index Data Reader.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

A bank must process chat requests inside the EU geography. The workload is interactive, billed per token, and does not need reserved capacity.

Which deployment type should you choose?
opts: Global Standard, with requests routed to any region
Data Zone Standard, with the EU data zone selected
Developer, with no service level agreement
normal.rationale: Data Zone Standard keeps processing inside the chosen data zone, here the EU, with pay-per-token billing. Global Standard can route requests to any region. Global Batch is asynchronous, and Developer is for testing.
normal.hint: Processing must stay in a geography = Data Zone. Anywhere = Global.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam. Microsoft Learn says the EU data zone follows the EU Data Boundary, which can include EFTA countries such as Norway and Switzerland.

choices: Request a tokens-per-minute quota increase for a Standard deployment
Estimate the required PTUs for the workload
Create a Global Batch deployment for the workload
Purchase an Azure reservation for the deployed PTUs
Verify that PTU capacity is available in the region

slots.label: Step 2
slots.correct: Verify that PTU capacity is available in the region
choices: Verify that PTU capacity is available in the region
Purchase an Azure reservation for the deployed PTUs
Request a tokens-per-minute quota increase for a Standard deployment
Create a Global Batch deployment for the workload
Estimate the required PTUs for the workload

slots.label: Step 3
choices: Purchase an Azure reservation for the deployed PTUs
Estimate the required PTUs for the workload
Request a tokens-per-minute quota increase for a Standard deployment
Verify that PTU capacity is available in the region
Create a Global Batch deployment for the workload

slots.label: Step 4
slots.correct: Purchase an Azure reservation for the deployed PTUs
choices: Create a Global Batch deployment for the workload
Estimate the required PTUs for the workload
Verify that PTU capacity is available in the region
Purchase an Azure reservation for the deployed PTUs
Request a tokens-per-minute quota increase for a Standard deployment

Which deployment option should you use?

normal.rationale: Serverless API deployments are billed per token and need no infrastructure from you. Managed compute runs on dedicated capacity billed by time. Provisioned throughput is billed for reserved capacity rather than per token, and batch processing is not meant for interactive calls.

Your production app uses a Standard deployment of a chat model. Behavior must not change when Microsoft designates a new default model version, until you have tested that version.

What should you configure?
opts: Set the deployment's version upgrade policy to OnceNewDefaultVersionAvailable
Pin the api-version in the SDK client
Set the deployment's version upgrade policy to NoAutoUpgrade
Set the deployment's version upgrade policy to OnceCurrentVersionExpired
normal.rationale: NoAutoUpgrade keeps the deployment on its current model version (until retirement). OnceNewDefaultVersionAvailable upgrades soon after a new default is designated, and OnceCurrentVersionExpired still upgrades at retirement.

normal.stem:
You have two variants of a system prompt. Before merging one into the main branch, you need an objective choice.

What should you do?
opts: Ask two reviewers to try three questions each, and pick by feel
Run both variants over the same test dataset with the same evaluators, and compare the scores
Merge the variant that has the longer prompt, because it contains more guidance
Deploy both to production, and decide after a month
normal.rationale: Running both variants on one fixed dataset with the same evaluators gives comparable numbers before anything ships. Length is not quality, three hand-picked questions are not a sample, and a month in production is not a pre-merge check.
normal.hint: Compare prompt variants = same dataset, same evaluators.

After an incident, the team must trace the exact prompt text that produced a bad answer in production.

Which approach supports that?
opts: Keep prompts as files in Git, deploy from a tagged commit, and log the commit SHA with each request
Store the prompt in a database row that any developer can edit, without a change log
Edit the prompt directly in the portal playground, and copy the final text to a wiki page
Keep the latest prompt text in a shared wiki page, and update it when it changes
normal.rationale: Prompts in Git are reviewed, versioned and reproducible, and the logged SHA ties each request to the exact text.
normal.hint: Prompts are code: Git + tag + log the version.

Foundry User, assigned at the Mortgage project scope
Foundry User, assigned at the subscription scope
Contributor, assigned at the resource group scope

Which built-in role is required to deploy the fine-tuned model?

normal.stem:
You run a local evaluation with the Azure AI Evaluation SDK. The JSONL file has the columns `question`, `answer` and `docs`. The Groundedness evaluator needs `response` and `context`.

Which column mapping is correct?
normal.rationale: In the SDK's evaluate() the mapping uses the ${data.column} syntax, and each evaluator input must point at the right column: the answer is the response and the retrieved documents are the context. The {{item.column}} syntax belongs to cloud evaluations, and the other mappings feed the wrong columns.

normal.stem:
You want to run the HateUnfairnessEvaluator, a built-in risk and safety evaluator, in the Azure AI Evaluation SDK.

What must you provide to the evaluator?
opts: A ground_truth column in the dataset
A model_config that points to a GPT deployment
The azure_ai_project information and a credential
Only an API key for Azure AI Content Safety, with no project information
normal.rationale: Risk and safety evaluators run on the Foundry safety evaluation service, so you give them the Foundry project (azure_ai_project) and a credential instead of a GPT model_config. They do not need ground truth.
normal.hint: Quality evaluators = model_config. Safety evaluators = azure_ai_project.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem: Match each evaluator to what it checks for an agent.

slots.label: Whether the agent called the right tools with the right parameters
Whether the agent correctly identified and addressed what the user wanted
Whether the agent's response follows the task and instructions it was assigned

normal.rationale: ToolCallAccuracy looks at tool selection and parameters, IntentResolution at whether the user's intent was understood and addressed, and TaskAdherence at whether the response sticks to the assigned task. Groundedness compares an answer with source context, which is not about agent behavior.
normal.hint: Tool calls = ToolCallAccuracy. User goal = IntentResolution. Follows instructions = TaskAdherence.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
You must verify that every response is 100 words or fewer. The check must be deterministic and cheap, and it must run in your automated evaluation workflow.

What should you create?
opts: A code-based custom evaluator: a Python callable that returns the word count result
The built-in Coherence evaluator, with the 100-word limit added to its prompt
A prompt-based custom evaluator that asks a GPT judge to count the words
The built-in Fluency evaluator, with a threshold of 3 on the response
normal.rationale: A length rule is a plain computation, so a code-based evaluator gives the same answer every time at no model cost, and it can be passed to evaluate() with the built-in ones. An LLM judge is slower, costs tokens and can miscount, and Fluency and Coherence do not measure length.
normal.hint: Rule you can compute = code-based custom evaluator. Judgment call = prompt-based.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
An evaluation of a RAG assistant gives the following average scores on a 1 to 5 scale (a score of 3 or more passes):

- Retrieval: 4.5
- Groundedness: 4.6
- Relevance: 2.1
- Fluency: 4.8

What should you do first?
opts: Reduce the chunk size and rebuild the search index with the new chunks
Add a stricter completion content filter to catch unrelated answers
Rewrite the generation prompt so answers address the user's question
Fine-tune the embedding model on the domain's query and document pairs
normal.rationale: Retrieval is high, so the right chunks are found. Groundedness is high, so the answers match those chunks, and fluency is high. Only Relevance fails, which means the answers do not address the question, so the problem is in the generation step. Chunking, embeddings and content filters would not fix it.
normal.hint: Read the scores as a chain: retrieval, then grounding, then relevance.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem: Which TWO built-in evaluators require ground truth data?
normal.rationale: F1 score compares the response with a ground-truth answer. Document Retrieval compares the retrieved documents with labeled relevant documents. Groundedness, Fluency and Relevance judge the response without labels.
normal.hint: Needs labels = F1 and Document Retrieval.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
You monitor an Azure OpenAI deployment that serves non-streaming requests. You need the overall response time, split by deployment.

Which metric should you chart?
opts: Processed Prompt Tokens, split by ModelDeploymentName
Time to Response, split by ModelDeploymentName
Time to Last Byte, split by ModelDeploymentName
normal.rationale: Time to Last Byte measures the total time until the last token is returned, which is the right overall latency for non-streaming calls. Time to Response measures how soon the first response appears and is recommended for streaming. The other two are token and capacity metrics, not latency.
normal.hint: Non-streaming latency = Time to Last Byte. Streaming first token = Time to Response.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
Users report that an assistant often misses a key sentence because the document was split between two consecutive chunks.

What should you change?
opts: Reduce the chunk size to one sentence, and remove the overlap
normal.rationale: Overlap repeats a small amount of text from one chunk in the next, which helps keep continuity and context across the boundary.
normal.hint: Facts cut at chunk boundaries = add overlap.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Chunk large documents for RAG and vector search in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)

normal.stem:
A hybrid query in Azure AI Search runs a keyword search and a vector search.

How are the two result lists combined?
opts: By averaging the raw keyword and vector scores
By returning all vector results first, followed by the keyword results
By using keyword results as filters on the vector results
With Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which merges the lists by rank position
normal.rationale: Keyword and vector scores are on different scales, so Azure AI Search merges the ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which uses rank positions rather than raw scores.
normal.hint: Hybrid search merges ranked lists with RRF.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Relevance scoring in hybrid search using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)

normal.stem:
A RAG app sends 20 chunks to the model for every question. Many of them are unrelated, which lowers groundedness and increases token cost.

Which change should you make at the retrieval stage?
opts: Add more few-shot examples that show the model how to ignore irrelevant chunks
Increase max_tokens so the model can explain which chunks are relevant
Raise the minimum similarity or reranker threshold, and reduce top-k
Increase top-k to 50 so that the right chunk is always included in context
normal.rationale: Filtering by a similarity or reranker threshold and sending fewer chunks removes noise before it reaches the model. More chunks add more noise and cost.
normal.hint: Too much noise in context = stricter threshold, smaller top-k.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Information retrieval

normal.stem:
A medical assistant retrieves documents poorly because a general-purpose embedding model does not capture the meaning of domain abbreviations. You have labeled pairs of queries and relevant documents.

What should you do?
opts: Lower the generation temperature so the model stays closer to the retrieved text
Increase top-k to 50 so more candidate documents reach the model
Switch the chat model to a larger model that understands the abbreviations better
Choose or fine-tune a domain embedding model, and re-embed the index and queries with it
normal.rationale: The weakness is in how text is turned into vectors, so the fix is a better embedding model, and the documents and queries must be embedded with the same new model.
normal.hint: Retrieval misses domain terms = domain embedding model, and re-embed everything.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: RAG generate embeddings phase

normal.stem: Which technique fits each requirement best?

slots.label: Answers must reflect policy documents that are updated every day
You have thousands of labeled examples and need a consistent output style and format, and the few-shot prompt has become too long
A few edge cases need a quick behavior change and you have no training data

normal.rationale: RAG brings in current or private knowledge at query time. Supervised fine-tuning teaches style, tone and format from examples and can shorten prompts. Fine-tuning needs task-specific training data, so a quick change with no data is made in the prompt. Fine-tuning does not keep facts up to date.
normal.hint: Facts that change = RAG. Style and format at scale = fine-tuning. Quick tweak = prompt.

sources.title: Training in Microsoft Foundry

normal.stem:
During fine-tuning, the training loss keeps falling but the validation loss starts to rise.

Which TWO changes can reduce the overfitting?
normal.rationale: Falling training loss with rising validation loss is a sign of overfitting. Fewer epochs and a smaller learning rate multiplier both reduce how strongly the model fits the training data. More epochs or a larger multiplier make it worse.
normal.hint: Overfitting = fewer epochs, lower learning rate multiplier.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Fine-tune a model with supervised fine-tuning in Microsoft Foundry

normal.stem:
A fine-tuning job saved checkpoints at the end of each epoch. The validation results are:

- Epoch 1: validation loss 0.92
- Epoch 2: validation loss 0.61
- Epoch 3: validation loss 0.68
- Epoch 4: validation loss 0.80

Which checkpoint should you deploy?
opts: The epoch 1 checkpoint, because it has been trained the least
Average the weights of the four checkpoints, and deploy the result
The epoch 2 checkpoint, after confirming it on held-out examples
The epoch 4 checkpoint, because it is the most recently saved
normal.rationale: Validation loss is lowest at epoch 2 and then rises, so later checkpoints overfit. The latest checkpoint is not automatically the best, so compare candidates and confirm on held-out examples.
normal.hint: Pick the checkpoint with the best validation result, not the latest.
normal.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

normal.stem:
You generated 2,000 training examples for fine-tuning by prompting a stronger model.

Which practice is recommended?
opts: Use the same generated examples for both training and validation, to save effort
Add the validation examples to the training set as well, to get more training data
Skip validation, because a stronger model produced the examples, so they are reliable
Review and filter the generated examples, and keep validation data separate from training data
normal.rationale: Synthetic data can contain errors, so it is reviewed and filtered. Training and validation examples are kept in separate files.
normal.hint: Synthetic data still needs review, and validation stays separate.

series.title: App Service calling a model deployment
series.text:
You have an Azure App Service web app that calls a model deployment in a Foundry resource.

**Goal.** The app must call the deployment without any stored secrets, using only the permissions needed for inference.

For each of the next three questions, read one proposed solution and decide whether it meets the goal.

qs.stem:
**Solution:** Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the web app, and assign it the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role on the Foundry resource.

Does the solution meet the goal?
qs.rationale: A managed identity means no secret is stored, and Cognitive Services OpenAI User allows calling model deployments without granting management rights, so it matches least privilege for inference.
qs.hint: Managed identity + a role that only allows inference = no secret, least privilege.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam. Microsoft Learn pages differ: the Azure OpenAI role page lets Cognitive Services OpenAI User make inference calls, while the Foundry role page says not to assign Cognitive Services roles for Foundry scenarios and names Foundry User for inference.

series.title: Cutting the cost of a hyperparameter sweep
series.text:
You run a sweep job in Azure Machine Learning. It tunes `learning_rate`, a continuous value, and `batch_size`, a discrete value. The training script logs the primary metric after every epoch.

**Goal.** Reduce compute cost by stopping poorly performing trials early, while still exploring the continuous range of `learning_rate`.

For each of the next three questions, read one proposed solution and decide whether it meets the goal.

qs.stem:
**Solution:** Use random sampling with a Bandit early termination policy (slack_factor 0.1, evaluation_interval 1, delay_evaluation 5).

Does the solution meet the goal?
qs.rationale: Random sampling supports continuous values, and the Bandit policy cancels trials that fall outside the slack factor of the best trial, so poor trials stop early and compute is saved.
qs.hint: Random sampling + an early termination policy.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Hyperparameter tuning a model (v2)

qs.stem:
**Solution:** Use grid sampling with `learning_rate` defined as a Uniform distribution, together with a Bandit early termination policy.

Does the solution meet the goal?
qs.rationale: Grid sampling supports only Choice values, so it cannot sample a continuous Uniform range. The policy is fine, but the sampling choice fails the requirement to explore the continuous range.
qs.hint: Grid = Choice only, so it cannot explore a continuous range.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

sources.title: Hyperparameter tuning a model (v2)

qs.stem:
**Solution:** Use random sampling, and set max_concurrent_trials equal to max_total_trials.

Does the solution meet the goal?
qs.rationale: Running all trials at once only changes parallelism. No trial is stopped early, so no compute is saved.
qs.hint: Parallelism is not early termination.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

cases.title: Fabrikam Insurance claims assistant
cases.text:
**Business.** Fabrikam Insurance is building a claims assistant for 2,000 adjusters. It is an agent in Microsoft Foundry that answers questions from policy documents indexed in Azure AI Search and can call one external partner API at `api.partnerco.example`.

**Workloads.**
- Adjusters chat with the agent during business hours. Usage peaks sharply at 9:00 and 14:00, and the business wants reserved capacity with predictable latency.
- A nightly job summarizes about 50,000 claim notes. Nothing needs the results before the next morning, and the business wants the lowest cost for this job.

**Security and governance.**
- The model, the search service and the storage account must not be reachable from the public internet. Traffic to them goes through private endpoints.
- The agent's only allowed internet destination is `api.partnerco.example`.
- External brokers upload policy PDFs that are indexed and later passed to the model as grounding documents. The security team is worried that a PDF may contain hidden instructions aimed at the model.
- The deployment pipeline runs in GitHub Actions. No long-lived secrets are allowed, and the risk team must approve production releases.

**Quality and operations.**
- The team has a test set of 300 questions. For each question, a reviewer labeled which policy documents are relevant.
- The team wants to catch answers that contain claims not supported by the retrieved policy text.
- Finance wants spend per department, and the platform team wants token counts per model deployment and traces of failed agent runs.

qs.stem: Which deployment type fits each workload?

slots.label: Adjuster chat: business-hours peaks, reserved capacity and predictable latency
Nightly summarization of 50,000 claim notes: asynchronous, results by next morning, lowest cost

qs.rationale: Provisioned throughput reserves model capacity (PTUs), which gives predictable latency for interactive traffic. Global Batch is asynchronous with a 24-hour target and costs about 50% less than standard, which suits a nightly job nobody waits on. Global Standard is pay-per-token with no reserved capacity, and Developer is meant for testing.
qs.hint: Interactive + reserved capacity = Provisioned throughput. Asynchronous + cheapest = Global Batch.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the bank's topics. It is not from the real exam, so treat the answer as our reasoning.

sources.title: Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models
What is provisioned throughput for Foundry Models?

qs.stem:
You need to restrict the agent's outbound internet access to `api.partnerco.example` only, while the Azure resources stay reachable through private endpoints.

What should you configure in the managed network?
opts: Set the isolation mode to Allow internet outbound, and add a private endpoint rule for the partner API
Set the isolation mode to Allow only approved outbound, and add an FQDN outbound rule for `api.partnerco.example`
Set the isolation mode to Allow only approved outbound, and add a service tag outbound rule for the partner API
Disable managed network isolation, and restrict access with a Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy
qs.rationale: Allow only approved outbound blocks everything except the rules you add. A public third-party hostname is allowed with an FQDN outbound rule. A private endpoint rule is for dependent Azure resources, and Allow internet outbound does not restrict anything.
qs.hint: Allow only a specific public hostname = Approved outbound + FQDN rule. Azure PaaS resources = private endpoint rule.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the bank's topics. It is not from the real exam, so treat the answer as our reasoning.

qs.stem:
The security team is worried about hidden instructions inside the uploaded policy PDFs that are passed to the model as grounding documents.

What should you configure?
opts: Enable Prompt Shields user prompt attack detection on the chat input of each request
Turn on indirect attack detection in Prompt Shields, with the policy text marked by delimiters
Set the completion content filter thresholds to the strictest level for the four harm categories
Set the prompt content filter thresholds to the strictest level for the four harm categories
qs.rationale: Hidden instructions inside documents are an indirect attack. Prompt Shields indirect attack detection looks at content marked as a document, so the grounding text must be delimited. User prompt attack detection covers jailbreak attempts typed by the user. Content filter thresholds, on the prompt or the completion, rate harm categories such as hate or violence, which is a different problem.
qs.hint: Attack hidden in a document = indirect attack detection + delimiters. Attack typed by the user = user prompt attack detection.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the bank's topics. It is not from the real exam, so treat the answer as our reasoning.

qs.stem: Which evaluator should the team use for each goal?

slots.label: Measure how well the retrieved documents match the reviewers' labeled relevant documents
Catch answers that contain claims not supported by the retrieved policy text

qs.rationale: Document Retrieval compares retrieved documents with labeled ground truth and reports ranking metrics such as NDCG, so it needs labels. Groundedness checks the answer against the retrieved context, so it flags unsupported claims. Retrieval and Relevance are judged by an LLM without labels, and Coherence and Fluency score the writing.
qs.hint: Labels for documents = Document Retrieval. Answer vs retrieved chunks = Groundedness.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the bank's topics. It is not from the real exam, so treat the answer as our reasoning.

qs.stem: Which tool gives each piece of information?

slots.label: Traces and failures of individual agent runs
Processed prompt tokens per model deployment
Spend per department, using resource tags

qs.rationale: Application Insights holds traces and failures. Token counts such as Processed Prompt Tokens are Azure Monitor metrics, and you can split them by ModelDeploymentName. Money, grouped by tag, is in Cost Analysis. The activity log records control-plane operations such as who changed a resource.
qs.hint: Traces and failures = App Insights. Token counts = Azure Monitor metrics. Money by tag = Cost Analysis.

cases.title: Northwind Retail demand forecasting
cases.text:
**Business.** Northwind Retail forecasts weekly demand per store with a model built and operated in Azure Machine Learning.

**Training.**
- Training data lives in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and is read as an `mltable` data asset.
- A pipeline retrains the model every week, using a hyperparameter sweep. Metrics are logged with MLflow, and the best model is registered in the workspace registry.
- Training runs on a compute cluster that must not cost money when no jobs are running.

**Serving.**
- The model is served by a managed online endpoint named `forecast-ep`. The `blue` deployment takes 100% of traffic.
- The scoring script reads a store-calendar file from a separate storage account named `stgcalendar` on every request. Security forbids storing account keys or SAS tokens anywhere in the solution.
- At peak hours some callers receive HTTP 429. Requests that send a full-region payload receive HTTP 504, because the deployment's request timeout is 5,000 ms and scoring those payloads takes about 8 seconds.
- Every weekly model must first be tested on real production requests before it serves a single customer response.

**Monitoring.**
- Actual sales for a week arrive about 30 days later.
- The team wants an early warning when the input features in production stop looking like the training data.

**Delivery.** The release workflow runs in GitHub Actions. It signs in to Azure with OpenID Connect and deploys to a protected `prod` environment that requires reviewer approval.

qs.stem:
Each weekly model must be tested on real production requests before it serves a single customer response.

How should you configure the `green` deployment that holds the new model?
opts: Set `traffic` to 100% for green, and keep blue deployed as a fallback
Set `mirror_traffic` to a share of live requests for green, and keep `traffic` at 100% for blue
Set `traffic` to 90% for blue and 10% for green, and watch the error rate
Move green to a batch endpoint, and replay exported production requests against it
qs.rationale: Mirrored traffic copies a share of live requests to green while the response always comes from the deployment that holds the live traffic, so customers never see green's output. A traffic split sends real responses to customers from green. A batch endpoint runs asynchronously over stored data.
qs.hint: Test on live requests with no customer impact = mirror_traffic. Real customers on the new version = traffic split.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the bank's topics. It is not from the real exam, so treat the answer as our reasoning.

qs.stem: Which deployment setting fixes each symptom?

slots.label: HTTP 429 at peak hours
HTTP 504 on full-region payloads that take about 8 seconds

qs.rationale: A 429 means the endpoint is receiving more requests than its instances can take, so you add instances. A 504 on slow requests means the request timed out, so you raise `request_timeout_ms` above the real scoring time (here more than 8,000 ms). The readiness probe delay affects startup, and a batch endpoint would remove real-time inference.
qs.hint: 429 = too many requests, add instances. 504 = request too slow, raise request_timeout_ms.

The scoring script must read the calendar file from `stgcalendar` on every request, and security forbids keys and SAS tokens.

What should you do?

Assign a managed identity to the endpoint, and grant it Storage Blob Data Reader on `stgcalendar`
Grant the data science group the Owner role on `stgcalendar`, and run the script as them
Generate a SAS token that expires in one year, and embed it in the scoring script
qs.rationale: A managed identity lets the scoring code authenticate without any secret, and Storage Blob Data Reader gives only read access to blobs, which is the least privilege the script needs. Account keys and SAS tokens are secrets, which the requirement forbids. Giving a group Owner is far too broad and does not give the endpoint an identity at all.

cases.title: Adventure Works Bank loan assistant
cases.text:
**Business.** Adventure Works Bank runs a loan-assistant agent in Microsoft Foundry for 400 loan officers. One Foundry resource hosts the model deployments, and each product team has its own project in it.

**People and access.**
- Developers in the Mortgage team build and run agents in the Mortgage project only.
- Internal auditors need read-only visibility of the resource configuration. They must not be able to run agents or change anything.

**Delivery.**
- Infrastructure is deployed with Bicep from GitHub Actions. The repository is `adventureworks/loan-infra`.
- Production deployments run in a protected GitHub environment named `prod`, which needs approval from the risk team.
- No client secrets are allowed. The Microsoft Entra app used by the workflow must only issue tokens to workflows that run in the `prod` environment of this repository.

**Network and identity.**
- The Foundry resource is not reachable from the public internet. Developers connect from the corporate network through a private endpoint.
- After the private endpoint was created, developers on the corporate network still resolve the Foundry endpoint name to a public IP address and are blocked.
- The agent reads loan policies from Azure AI Search and customer documents from Blob Storage. The Mortgage and Auto projects must use the same identity, and that identity must survive if a project is deleted and recreated.

**Governance.** Security wants to guarantee that nobody in any subscription can create a Foundry resource with public network access enabled.

qs.stem:
You need to create the federated credential on the Microsoft Entra app. It must issue tokens only to workflows that run in the `prod` environment of `adventureworks/loan-infra`. The repository uses GitHub's name-based subject format.

Which subject should you use?
qs.rationale: The environment subject has the form repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:<name>, so it must name the prod environment exactly. This is the name-based format; repositories created, renamed or transferred from July 15, 2026 use a format that adds the owner and repository IDs, and older ones keep this format until they opt in. A branch subject matches any workflow on main whether or not it runs in the protected environment, a pull request subject matches pull request runs, and environment:production is a different name from prod.
qs.hint: OIDC subject for an environment = repo:org/repo:environment:name.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

qs.stem: Which role assignment should each group receive? Choose the one that follows least privilege.

slots.label: Mortgage developers: build and run agents, only in the Mortgage project
slots.correct: Foundry User at the Mortgage project
choices: Foundry User at the Mortgage project

slots.label: Auditors: read-only view of the resource configuration, nothing else
choices: Foundry Owner at the Foundry resource

qs.rationale: Foundry User (formerly Azure AI User) at the project scope lets developers build there without touching other projects. Reader at the resource shows configuration without allowing changes. The other combinations either give broader scope or write access.
qs.hint: Developers: Foundry User at project scope. Auditors: Reader.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

qs.stem:
The Mortgage and Auto projects must use the same identity to read from Azure AI Search and Blob Storage, and the identity must survive if a project is deleted and recreated.

Which identity should you use?
opts: A system-assigned managed identity enabled separately on each of the two projects
The sign-in identity of the developer who created the projects, used by the agents
A service principal with a client secret that is stored in each project's connection
A user-assigned managed identity, created separately and attached to both projects
qs.rationale: A user-assigned managed identity is its own Azure resource, so it can be shared and keeps its role assignments when a project is deleted. A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and is deleted with it. A client secret is a secret, and a developer's identity should not be used by an application.
qs.hint: Shared and long-lived identity = user-assigned managed identity.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

qs.stem:
Security wants to guarantee that nobody in any subscription can create a Foundry resource with public network access enabled.

What should you do?
opts: Assign an Azure Policy with the Deny effect for public network access, at the management group scope
Ask each team to check the network setting after deployment, and report exceptions
Create a network security group rule that blocks inbound internet traffic to the Foundry resource
Assign an Azure Policy with the Audit effect, and review the compliance report every month
qs.rationale: A Deny policy blocks the creation or update of non-compliant resources, and assigning it at the management group scope covers every subscription under it. Manual checks do not guarantee anything.
qs.hint: Prevent = Azure Policy with Deny. Report only = Audit.
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.

qs.stem:
Developers on the corporate network still resolve the Foundry endpoint name to a public IP address and are blocked.

What should you do?
opts: Add an FQDN outbound rule to the managed network for the Foundry hostname
Assign a public IP address to the private endpoint network interface
Enable public network access on the Foundry resource for the corporate IP range
Link a private DNS zone to the virtual network, and forward corporate DNS queries to it
qs.rationale: A private endpoint only works when the service name resolves to its private IP. A private DNS zone linked to the network, with corporate DNS forwarding to it, does that (Foundry uses zones such as privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com, privatelink.openai.azure.com and privatelink.services.ai.azure.com). Enabling public access defeats the requirement, and an outbound FQDN rule affects traffic leaving a managed network.
qs.hint: Private endpoint + wrong IP = fix DNS (private DNS zone).
qs.note: Synthetic question written by Claude from the official skills outline and the docs. It is not from the real exam.
